name: Kinematic Video and Generated Movement
title: Kinematic Video and Generated Movement
answer: Kinematic video and generated movement covers systems that read recorded human motion from video, estimate joint positions over time, and produce new movement sequences for dance, theatre, animation, or physical training. It sits between choreography and motion mapping, treating a dancer's body as a data source rather than only as a performer. The page includes pose estimation, motion transfer, and generative models that output movement notation, animation rigs, or video. It does not cover static pose recognition or full character animation pipelines outside human movement.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard computer vision stacks: a camera or video file feeds a pose estimation model that returns skeletal keypoints frame by frame. Generated movement models typically run on a single GPU for inference, though training may require larger compute. Output can be a sequence of joint angles, a motion capture file, or rendered video. Many practitioners use open source pose libraries and motion datasets, but this page does not yet track any specific live models or tools.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical workflow starts with extracting 2D or 3D joint positions from video using a pose estimator. Those keypoint sequences are then normalized, cleaned, and sometimes mapped onto a standard skeleton. A generative model, often a transformer or diffusion model trained on motion capture data, learns to continue, interpolate, or remix the movement. The result is reviewed by a choreographer or animator, who may adjust timing, weight, or style before it is used in performance.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions are unsettled. A dancer recorded for training data may not have agreed to their movement being used to generate new work, and choreographic style can be copied without credit. Provenance is hard to trace because generated motion is a statistical blend, not a direct copy. Practitioners should document the source video, the model, and the human edits, and should get clear consent from performers before using their movement in a training set. This page describes practice and is not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Generated movement is moving from short, looping clips toward longer sequences that respond to music, text, or another dancer in real time. Better 3D pose estimation from ordinary cameras will lower the barrier for small companies and independent choreographers. The next step is likely hybrid workflows where a human improvises, the system proposes variations, and the choreographer selects and refines them, rather than fully automated dance generation.
